common.tagline: Learn to say no. Live your life.

landing.heroSub: A personalized program to help you build healthy boundaries, say no confidently, and stop living for others' approval.
landing.feature1Desc: Take a science-backed diagnostic to uncover the root causes of your people-pleasing behavior.
landing.feature2Desc: Get personalized CBT-based guidance from your AI coach — available 24/7.
landing.feature3Desc: Build new habits with daily exercises designed for real-life situations.
landing.trust: Trusted by thousands. Science-backed. Private & anonymous.

onboarding.step1Sub: Tell us a bit about yourself so we can personalize your program.
onboarding.step4Sub: Let's start with a quick diagnostic to understand where you are today.

diagnostic.title: Boundary Diagnostic
diagnostic.subtitle: 20 questions · ~5 minutes
diagnostic.instruction: Answer honestly — there are no right or wrong answers.
diagnostic.resultDesc: Based on your answers, here is your profile:
diagnostic.mildDesc: You have a good foundation of self-awareness. Small adjustments will strengthen your boundaries significantly.
diagnostic.moderateDesc: You show clear people-pleasing patterns that are costing you energy and authenticity. Your 30-day program is designed for exactly where you are.
diagnostic.severeDesc: You are in a chronic pattern of self-abandonment. This is not your fault — it's learned behavior. Your program will work from the ground up.
diagnostic.q1: I say yes to requests even when I don't want to.
diagnostic.q2: I feel anxious when someone might be upset with me.
diagnostic.q3: I apologize even when I haven't done anything wrong.
diagnostic.q4: I prioritize other people's needs over my own.
diagnostic.q5: I find it hard to express my true opinions in groups.
diagnostic.q6: I feel guilty when I spend time on myself.
diagnostic.q7: I avoid conflict even when it hurts me.
diagnostic.q8: I change my behavior based on who I'm with.
diagnostic.q9: I feel responsible for other people's emotions.
diagnostic.q10: I have trouble asking for help or favors.
diagnostic.q11: I stay in uncomfortable situations to avoid disappointing others.
diagnostic.q12: I feel resentful but say nothing about it.
diagnostic.q13: I over-explain my decisions to justify myself.
diagnostic.q14: I struggle to make decisions without others' input.
diagnostic.q15: I feel like my needs don't matter as much as others'.
diagnostic.q16: I take on extra work to avoid being seen as lazy.
diagnostic.q17: I fear being seen as selfish if I put myself first.
diagnostic.q18: I rehearse conversations in my head to avoid conflict.
diagnostic.q19: I feel empty or resentful after helping others.
diagnostic.q20: I struggle to end relationships that drain me.

settings.title: Settings
settings.notificationsDesc: Get a daily nudge to practice your boundaries
settings.resetWarning: This will delete all your data. This cannot be undone.
settings.genderDesc: How should your coach address you?
settings.genderNeutralNote: Your coach will use neutral, inclusive language and avoid gendered assumptions.

ex.1_desc: Today, notice every time you say yes to something. Don't change your behavior yet — just observe.
ex.1_scenario: Your colleague asks you to help with their report after hours.
ex.1_bad: Sure, no problem! I'll stay late.
ex.1_good: I notice I want to immediately say yes. Let me pause and check if I actually have the capacity.
ex.1_tip: Awareness is the first step. You can't change what you don't notice.
ex.2_desc: Before agreeing to anything today, do a 3-second body scan. Notice tension, tightness, or discomfort.
ex.2_scenario: A friend asks you to help them move this weekend.
ex.2_bad: Of course! I'll be there at 8am.
ex.2_good: I feel a knot in my stomach — that's my signal that I'm overcommitting.
ex.2_tip: Your body often knows your true answer before your mind does.
ex.3_desc: Write down every yes you said today. Rate each one: Did you really want to? 1=No, 5=Yes.
ex.3_scenario: Someone asks you to join a committee at work.
ex.3_good: I said yes, but I rated it 1. I didn't want to but feared looking unhelpful.
ex.3_tip: Journaling reveals patterns that are invisible in the moment.
ex.4_desc: Who or what makes you most likely to say yes against your will? Make a list.
ex.4_scenario: Your boss asks you to take on an extra project.
ex.4_good: Authority figures are my trigger. I say yes out of fear, not choice.
ex.4_tip: Knowing your triggers lets you prepare, not just react.
ex.5_desc: When you imagine saying no, what are you afraid of? Write down your top 3 fears.
ex.5_scenario: Your mother asks you to visit every Sunday.
ex.5_good: My fear: she'll be hurt. Deeper fear: she'll love me less. Root: I tie love to compliance.
ex.5_tip: Naming the fear removes much of its power.
ex.6_desc: Think of 3 times you said yes when you didn't want to. What did it cost you — time, energy, resentment?
ex.6_scenario: You agreed to work overtime for the third week in a row.
ex.6_bad: I was just being a team player.
ex.6_good: That yes cost me my weekend, my sleep, and my patience with my family.
ex.6_tip: Every yes to someone else is a no to yourself.
ex.7_desc: Review your week. What did you discover about your people-pleasing patterns? Write a 5-sentence summary.
ex.7_scenario: You look back at the week's journal entries.
ex.7_bad: I didn't really notice anything different.
ex.7_good: I noticed: I say yes most to authority, I feel fear first, and my body signals when I'm lying to myself.
ex.7_tip: Self-knowledge is not self-criticism. You're gathering data, not judging yourself.
ex.8_desc: Today, when asked anything non-urgent, pause for 5 seconds before responding. Say: 'Let me think about that.'
ex.8_scenario: A friend asks if you can babysit tomorrow night.
ex.8_good: Let me think about that for a moment... Actually, tomorrow doesn't work for me.
ex.8_tip: The pause breaks the automatic yes reflex. It signals you have choice.
ex.9_desc: Practice these phrases: 'I appreciate you asking, but I can't', 'That doesn't work for me', 'I'm not available.'
ex.9_scenario: A coworker asks you to cover their shift.
ex.9_bad: Oh, I guess I could... maybe.
ex.9_good: I appreciate you asking, but I'm not available that day.
ex.9_tip: A soft no is still a no. You don't need an excuse or explanation.
ex.10_desc: Notice how often you apologize unnecessarily. Today, replace 'I'm sorry but...' with 'I won't be able to...'
ex.10_scenario: You need to decline a social invitation.
ex.10_bad: I'm so sorry, I really wish I could come, I feel terrible...
ex.10_good: I won't be able to make it this time. Thanks for the invite.
ex.10_tip: Apologizing for having needs teaches others your needs don't matter.
ex.11_desc: Practice repeating your no calmly when someone pushes back. Same message, same tone, three times.
ex.11_scenario: Someone keeps insisting after you've said no.
ex.11_bad: Well... if you really need me... I suppose I could...
ex.11_good: 'I understand this is important to you, but I can't.' (×3, calmly)
ex.11_tip: Persistence from others doesn't obligate a different answer from you.
ex.12_desc: Practice this script for any request: 'I'll check my schedule and get back to you by [time].'
ex.12_scenario: Your manager asks you to lead a new initiative.
ex.12_bad: Yes, of course, happy to do it!
ex.12_good: I'd like to review my current workload first. Can I get back to you by tomorrow?
ex.12_tip: Time to reflect = better decisions. Impulse yeses cost you.
ex.13_desc: Write your top 5 personal values. Before each decision this week, check: does this align with my values?
ex.13_scenario: You're asked to work on a project you find meaningless.
ex.13_good: This conflicts with my value of meaningful work. That's useful information.
ex.13_tip: Your values are your internal compass for decisions.
ex.14_desc: Which new communication tools felt natural? Which felt impossible? Write about one successful moment.
ex.14_scenario: You reflect on your first 'real no' this week.
ex.14_bad: I didn't really manage to say no to anyone.
ex.14_good: I used the pause once and bought time twice. My first small victory.
ex.14_tip: Progress is not perfection. Celebrate every small step.
ex.15_desc: Identify 3 absolute boundaries: things you will not accept under any circumstances in each life area.
ex.15_scenario: A family member constantly criticizes your life choices.
ex.15_bad: I just try to ignore it.
ex.15_good: My boundary: I will not accept personal criticism. I will leave the room or end the call when it happens.
ex.15_tip: Boundaries without consequences are just wishes.
ex.16_desc: Practice: 'When you X, I feel Y. I need Z. If X continues, I will do A.'
ex.16_scenario: Your partner interrupts you constantly during conversations.
ex.16_good: When you interrupt me, I feel unheard. I need you to let me finish. If it continues, I'll pause the conversation.
ex.16_tip: This formula is specific, calm, and actionable — not a threat, a promise.
ex.17_desc: List the emotional work you do that others don't notice. Who relies on you for their emotional regulation?
ex.17_scenario: A friend calls you in crisis every week.
ex.17_bad: I'm always there for them, that's what friends do.
ex.17_good: I'm providing constant emotional support that is exhausting me. This is unsustainable without reciprocity.
ex.17_tip: Recognizing emotional labor is the first step to redistributing it.
ex.18_desc: Set one small boundary today and notice the response. Did the relationship survive? What happened?
ex.18_scenario: A friend asks for a favor you don't have capacity for.
ex.18_good: I can't right now. The friend was disappointed, but the friendship is intact.
ex.18_tip: Most relationships survive boundaries. Those that don't weren't healthy.
ex.19_desc: Audit your digital availability. Do you respond to messages immediately? Set response time expectations.
ex.19_scenario: Your boss messages you at 10pm expecting immediate responses.
ex.19_bad: I always reply right away so they know I'm dedicated.
ex.19_good: I set a status: 'I respond to messages during working hours (9–6pm).'
ex.19_tip: Availability without limits trains others to expect unlimited access.
ex.20_desc: For each guilt feeling today: is this yours to own, or someone else's responsibility?
ex.20_scenario: A family member is upset you can't come to an event.
ex.20_bad: I feel terrible. I should probably cancel my plans.
ex.20_good: Their disappointment is real and valid. But it's their emotion, not my responsibility to fix.
ex.20_tip: Guilt is information. But it's not always accurate.
ex.21_desc: Which boundary felt most important to set? What did you learn about the people in your life?
ex.21_scenario: Reflect on the boundaries set this week.
ex.21_bad: I still felt guilty about everything.
ex.21_good: I set 3 boundaries. Two went well. One caused friction — and that friction revealed something important.
ex.21_tip: Friction is not failure. It's data about the relationship.
ex.22_desc: Learn the difference: Aggressive = my needs at your expense. Assertive = my needs, your needs, both matter.
ex.22_scenario: A colleague takes credit for your work in a meeting.
ex.22_bad: I say nothing and seethe internally.
ex.22_good: 'Actually, I developed that solution — happy to walk through it.' (Calm, factual, firm.)
ex.22_tip: Assertiveness isn't selfish — it's honest. It models self-respect.
ex.23_desc: Practice: instead of yes or no, offer an alternative that works for you.
ex.23_scenario: You're asked to work late on a project.
ex.23_good: I can't stay late, but I can prioritize this first thing tomorrow morning. Will that work?
ex.23_tip: A counter-offer shows collaboration without self-sacrifice.
ex.24_desc: Make 3 requests today without apologizing for making them.
ex.24_scenario: You need quiet time to focus at work.
ex.24_bad: Sorry to bother you, I was wondering if maybe you could... sorry.
ex.24_good: I need 2 hours of uninterrupted time this afternoon. Can we schedule calls for the morning?
ex.24_tip: Apologizing for your needs signals they're not legitimate.
ex.25_desc: Reframe: conflict isn't a threat — it's two people trying to be honest. Practice expressing disagreement.
ex.25_scenario: A friend suggests a plan you genuinely dislike.
ex.25_good: Honestly, that's not really my thing. What about an alternative?
ex.25_tip: Authentic disagreement deepens relationships. False agreement erodes them.
ex.26_desc: After stating your position, stop talking. Resist the urge to fill silence or backtrack.
ex.26_scenario: You've asked for a raise. Your manager is quiet.
ex.26_bad: I mean, it's okay if not, I understand, I'm happy either way...
ex.26_good: State your ask. Then stop. Let the silence work.
ex.26_tip: Over-talking undermines your position. Silence is confident.
ex.27_desc: Write: Who am I when I'm not trying to please anyone? Describe yourself fully.
ex.27_scenario: You imagine a day where no one needs anything from you.
ex.27_bad: I don't really know who I am outside of helping others.
ex.27_good: Without performing for others, I am: curious, decisive, funny, creative, a bit introverted.
ex.27_tip: Your identity exists independent of others' approval.
ex.28_desc: Write a letter to the younger version of you who first learned to people-please. What would you tell them?
ex.28_scenario: You're writing to yourself at the age when this all started.
ex.28_bad: I wouldn't know what to say.
ex.28_good: Dear younger me: Your love was never conditional on your performance. You were always enough.
ex.28_tip: Compassion for your past self heals the root, not just the symptoms.
ex.29_desc: Write a personal manifesto: your rights, your values, your non-negotiables. Keep it.
ex.29_scenario: You're writing your personal rules for life.
ex.29_good: I have the right to: say no, change my mind, make mistakes, take up space, be imperfect.
ex.29_tip: Writing your values makes them real and defensible.
ex.30_desc: Write your before-and-after. Who were you on Day 1? Who are you now? What will you do differently?
ex.30_bad: I still have a long way to go.
ex.30_good: I am not the same person who started this. I know my patterns, I have tools, and I believe I deserve better.
ex.30_tip: You've done the work. This is not the end — it's your new baseline.
